title: Applied anatomy: the shoulder joint, rotator cuff and axillary nerve

guidelineVersions: BESS/BOA Patient Care Pathway: traumatic anterior shoulder instability (2015)
Robinson et al., J Bone Joint Surg Am (2006, 2012)

related.why: Shoulder examination: the clinical tests for the cuff muscles named here

brief.scenario: Finlay Campbell, 32, fell onto his outstretched right arm in a rugby tackle. Radiographs show an anterior dislocation of the shoulder. The examiner will ask you about the anatomy of the shoulder joint and the axillary nerve, and will read out any examination and radiograph findings you ask for.
brief.task: Answer the examiner's questions on the anatomy of the shoulder, the structures at risk in this injury and his early management.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: Joint and its stabilisers, the cuff, then the axillary nerve and what dislocation damages.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Reducing before documenting axillary nerve function.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "A ball-and-socket synovial joint that trades stability for movement."

grid.label: Joint and stability
grid.fail: Cannot say why the shoulder dislocates easily.
grid.pass: Ball-and-socket synovial joint: large head, shallow glenoid. Stabilised by labrum, capsule, glenohumeral ligaments and the rotator cuff.
grid.high: Separates static stabilisers (labrum, capsule, ligaments) from dynamic ones (cuff, long head of biceps); weakest anteroinferiorly, where it dislocates.

grid.label: Rotator cuff
grid.pass: Supraspinatus (abduction), infraspinatus and teres minor (external rotation), subscapularis (internal rotation).
grid.high: Adds insertions (greater tuberosity; subscapularis on lesser) and nerves: suprascapular, axillary to teres minor, upper and lower subscapular.

grid.label: Axillary nerve
grid.fail: Cannot name the nerve at risk or test it.
grid.pass: Posterior cord, C5 and C6. Passes through the quadrangular space and round the surgical neck. Supplies deltoid, teres minor and the regimental badge skin.
grid.high: Names quadrangular space borders: teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, humerus; posterior circumflex humeral artery runs with it.

grid.label: Structures damaged
grid.fail: Cannot describe any bony or labral injury.
grid.pass: Bankart lesion: anteroinferior labrum torn from the glenoid. Hill-Sachs lesion: impaction of the posterolateral humeral head.
grid.high: Adds that cuff tears, tuberosity fractures and nerve injuries often coexist, especially over 60; checks cuff function if a nerve deficit is found.

grid.label: Safe reduction
grid.fail: Reduces without documenting neurovascular status or excluding a fracture.
grid.pass: Documents axillary nerve and distal pulses first; pre-reduction radiographs to exclude fracture; analgesia or sedation; repeat examination and radiographs after.
grid.high: Recognises a proximal humeral neck fracture needs orthopaedic reduction, not ED manipulation; uses two radiographic views to confirm reduction.

grid.label: Recurrence and follow-up
grid.pass: Sling for comfort, early physiotherapy, fracture clinic follow-up; explains recurrence is high in young active men.
grid.high: Quantifies it: about 56% redislocate within 2 years at age 15 to 35; offers shoulder surgeon review for stabilisation.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's a hinge joint between the humerus and the scapula.

fail.speaker: examiner
fail.text: What damage does dislocation cause inside the joint?

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: It's usually just a soft-tissue stretch.

fail.speaker: candidate
fail.text: I'd pull it back in straight away and send him home in a sling.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A ball-and-socket synovial joint with a large head in a shallow glenoid. The labrum, capsule, glenohumeral ligaments and rotator cuff hold it stable.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Supraspinatus for abduction, infraspinatus and teres minor for external rotation, subscapularis for internal rotation.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: The axillary nerve, from the posterior cord, C5 and C6. It goes through the quadrangular space and round the surgical neck. I'd test deltoid and sensation over the regimental badge area.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: A Bankart lesion, where the anteroinferior labrum tears off the glenoid, and a Hill-Sachs lesion, an impaction on the posterolateral humeral head.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Document nerve and pulses, check radiographs exclude a fracture, then reduce under analgesia or sedation. Re-examine and X-ray afterwards.

pass.speaker: candidate
pass.text: Sling, physiotherapy and fracture clinic. I'd warn him that recurrence is high in young active men.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The static stabilisers are the labrum, capsule and ligaments; the dynamic ones are the cuff and long head of biceps. It's weakest anteroinferiorly.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tuberosity; subscapularis on the lesser. Suprascapular nerve for the first two, axillary for teres minor, subscapular nerves for subscapularis.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The nerve leaves the axilla through a four-sided gap below the joint capsule. Name that space, its borders and what passes with the nerve.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: The quadrangular space. Teres minor above, teres major below, the long head of triceps medially and the humerus laterally. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through it.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: He's 32. Would it matter if he were 70?

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Yes. Cuff tears, tuberosity fractures and nerve injuries often coexist, and are more frequent over 60. If there's a nerve deficit I'd check the cuff too.

high.speaker: examiner
high.text: The radiograph shows a neck of humerus fracture.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: Then I wouldn't manipulate in ED. It needs orthopaedic reduction. After any reduction I'd confirm it on two views.

high.speaker: candidate
high.text: At his age about 56% redislocate within 2 years, so I'd arrange review by a shoulder surgeon to discuss stabilisation.

failures.move: Reducing before documenting axillary nerve function.
failures.consequence: A nerve palsy cannot then be attributed to the injury or the reduction.
Can displace an undisplaced humeral neck fracture.

failures.move: Ignoring the cuff in an older patient.
failures.consequence: Misses a cuff tear that coexists with nerve injury and needs early repair.
Misses deltoid weakness, the motor sign of axillary nerve injury.

recovery.line: SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis.
Nerve and pulses first, radiographs, reduce, then re-examine and re-image.

knowledge.fact: Axillary nerve: posterior cord, C5 and C6; quadrangular space; deltoid, teres minor, regimental badge skin.
Quadrangular space: teres minor, teres major, long head of triceps, surgical neck of humerus.
Bankart: anteroinferior labral avulsion. Hill-Sachs: posterolateral humeral head impaction.
Cuff tear, tuberosity fracture and nerve deficit often coexist after anterior dislocation, more so over 60.
Age 15 to 35: recurrent instability in 55.7% within 2 years of a first dislocation.

recall.think: Axillary nerve palsy; missed fracture or cuff tear.
recall.say: "I'll document axillary nerve function before reduction."
do: Test deltoid and regimental badge sensation

numbers.meaning: recurrence within 2 years at age 15 to 35

recall.trap: Normal sensation does not exclude deltoid weakness.
recall.finish: Sling, physiotherapy, fracture clinic; shoulder surgeon review if young or recurrent.

partner.opening: Describe the shoulder joint and what keeps it stable.

reveals.finding: Read out: sensation over the regimental badge area is intact; deltoid contraction is palpable.

reveals.trigger: Examiner moves to the course of the axillary nerve
reveals.finding: Read out: in a dissection of the right shoulder viewed from behind, a nerve and its companion artery leave the axilla through a four-sided gap just below the joint capsule, then wind round the back of the humerus just below its head, deep to deltoid.
Read out: the AP and axillary views show the humeral head lying anterior and inferior to the glenoid, beneath the coracoid. No fracture is seen.

reveals.trigger: Candidate asks about the post-reduction radiograph
reveals.finding: Read out: the humeral head now sits congruently in the glenoid. There is a wedge-shaped notch in the posterolateral humeral head.

push.question: Name the rotator cuff and their nerves.
Which nerve is at risk and how would you test it?
push.expect: Axillary: deltoid and regimental badge sensation.

push.question: What is a Bankart lesion?
push.expect: Anteroinferior labrum torn from the glenoid.

push.question: What would you do before reducing?
push.expect: Document nerve and pulses, radiographs to exclude fracture, analgesia.

push.question: What will you tell him about the future?
push.expect: High recurrence in young men; physiotherapy; shoulder surgeon review.

curveballs.prompt: After reduction he cannot abduct; sensation is normal.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider axillary nerve palsy or a cuff tear; document, and arrange early imaging and specialist review.

curveballs.prompt: The pre-reduction radiographs show a fracture through the surgical neck.
curveballs.safeAnswer: Do not manipulate in ED; refer for orthopaedic reduction.

curveballs.prompt: What is the notch on the humeral head?
curveballs.safeAnswer: A Hill-Sachs lesion: impaction against the anterior glenoid rim.
